title: Direct Network Flood Detection across IaaS, Linux, Windows, and macOS
shortTitle: Direct Network Flood Detection across IaaS, Linux, Window...
summary: This detection strategy covers Direct Network Flood (T1498.001), where an adversary aims a high volume of traffic at one host, service or network link to exhaust bandwidth or connection state. The technique matters because it degrades or removes availability for real users, and because the traffic is often sourced from many hosts so per host thresholds stay quiet. The telemetry that makes it visible is flow level records such as NetFlow or IPFIX, cloud virtual private network flow logs, load balancer and edge device metrics, and interface counters on servers. The main failure mode is a poorly set baseline, because backup jobs, video calls, software updates and content distribution traffic all look like floods for a short time.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for a sudden flood of network traffic aimed at one target. The traffic comes from many sources at the same time. The goal of the flood is to make a service too busy to answer real users.
beginner.whyItMatters: A flood stops people from working, so the impact is immediate and visible to everyone. It can hide a quieter attack that runs at the same time. The traffic is hard to trace because it comes from many places. A good rule tells you which service is under pressure in the first minutes. That head start decides whether you can filter the traffic or must fail over to a backup site.
howItWorks: Network devices and cloud platforms summarise traffic into flow records, which describe conversations between hosts.
Each record carries the source, the destination, the port, the number of packets and the number of bytes.
The rule groups those records by destination and by short time windows, such as one minute.
It compares the rate in each window with the normal rate for that destination from the last few weeks.
A rate far above the baseline, especially with many distinct sources, raises an alert.
An analyst checks whether a planned event or a software rollout can explain the change.
beginner.example: Think of a shop with one till and one queue. Twenty normal shoppers are fine. Three hundred people arriving at once stop real customers from paying. The shop does not need to know every person in the crowd to know it has a problem. The flow record is the queue count at the door.
takeaways: Compare the current rate with a learned baseline instead of a fixed number.
Many sources hitting one destination is the strongest sign of a flood.
Check the change calendar before you call it an attack.

objectives: Explain how a direct network flood consumes bandwidth or connection state for a target
Identify flow, edge device and cloud telemetry that exposes a volumetric attack
Build a per destination and per service baseline that accounts for backups and updates
Write a rule that alerts on rate change and source diversity rather than a single traffic value
Triage the alert by confirming with service owners and checking the change calendar
Describe the coverage gap when only one telemetry source, such as flow records, is available
dataSources: NetFlow or IPFIX flow records exported from routers and switches with packets, bytes and source counts
Cloud virtual private network flow logs for inbound traffic to internet facing instances
Edge load balancer and firewall metrics showing connection rate, request rate and dropped packets per target
Server interface counters collected over SNMP showing inbound throughput per network interface
Cloud provider denial of service protection notices and autoscaling events for affected services
logic: The pattern is a sharp rise in inbound packet and connection rate against a single destination or service, sustained across several short windows and arriving from an unusually wide set of source addresses. The fields that must be correlated are the destination address and port, the observed packet and byte rates, the count of distinct sources, the protocol flags and the time of day. The benign case is a scheduled backup, a large software update, a video event or a content delivery surge that starts at a known time and comes from a small set of known networks. The malicious case is a sudden many to one pattern with high packet counts, uniform packet sizes, spoofed or scattered sources and no corresponding change record.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Volumetric Inbound Flood Against Single Service
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     flow_direction: inbound
#     packets_per_second: '>20000'
#     distinct_sources: '>200'
#   filter_planned:
#     change_window: maintenance
#   condition: selection and not filter_planned
# level: high
falsePositives: Nightly backup or replication jobs that push a large volume from a small set of known servers
A software update rollout that pulls a new package to thousands of endpoints at the same hour
A public marketing event or product launch that creates a genuine traffic spike on a web service
A monitoring system retrying a health check in a tight loop after a dependency fails
tuningNotes: Set the rule on a per destination baseline and group by service, because a shared threshold will either miss small floods or alert on busy but healthy services. Exclude known update, backup and content distribution networks by address range, and suppress destinations that are covered by a cloud protection service which already absorbs the traffic. Baseline weekly peaks first, then alert on the deviation rather than on the raw number. Narrowing this way reduces false pages a great deal, but a slow flood that stays just under the baseline, or a flood aimed at a service with no flow telemetry, will not alert, so keep interface counters as a second opinion.
